title: A handshake test tells true messengers from false ones
setting: On 9 February 1843, several visitors called at Joseph Smith’s home in Nauvoo. Parley and Orson Pratt were among them; Parley had returned to the city two days before. Joseph talked with them informally about how to tell true heavenly messengers from false ones. He had taught similar ideas in 1839, while Parley was jailed in Missouri. William Clayton and Willard Richards both recorded the remarks. Orson Pratt adapted Clayton’s version for the 1876 Doctrine and Covenants.
summary: These instructions say there are two kinds of beings in heaven. Angels are resurrected and have bodies of flesh and bones, as Jesus said of himself. The spirits of just men made perfect are not resurrected but share the same glory. When a messenger claims to come from God, ask him to shake hands. An angel will do so, and you will feel his hand. A just spirit will not move, because deceiving is against heaven’s order, but he will still give his message. If the devil comes as an angel of light, you will feel nothing and can detect him. The section calls these “three grand keys” for judging any messenger.

contextNote.title: Detecting a counterfeit messenger
contextNote.text: Joseph Smith had taught about discerning messengers as early as 1839. Verse 8 gives the test for a deceiver: he offers his hand, but nothing is felt. The test works because verses 1–3 first define what real messengers are. An angel has a body and can be touched, as verse 5 says. A just spirit will not pretend to have one, because that is “contrary to the order of heaven” (verse 7). Only the deceiver tries to seem what he is not. In this passage, a “key” is a practical test that exposes a false appearance.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 129–132 includes this section in its week but focuses on sections 130 and 132. Why does verse 7 say a just spirit will not shake hands, and how does that make the test in verse 8 work?
